source_title: Premium: AI Is Getting Way Too Expensive
other_side: Zitron's objection is not to any particular essay in the Thesis Statements collection — it is to the genre. He opens this piece by arguing that the whole discussion of AI's relationship to jobs, benefits and productivity is theoretical, that Anthropic's Economic Index and OpenAI's Economic Research Exchange are "marketing operations" propagating a belief for which little evidence exists, and that Anthropic's own head of economics has conceded "no material increase in the unemployment rate to date". His charge is that this conversation is "masturbatory and a conscious attempt to avoid" the messier one: roughly $110bn of trailing twelve-month revenue across the entire industry against hundreds of billions in commitments. Where NLW hears a hundred practitioners finally getting specific about work after automation, Zitron hears a hundred people describing a future underwritten by money that does not yet exist.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether the reorganisation of work now being described is being driven by capability or by capital. Both accept that agents do useful work today, that headline job losses have not yet appeared in the aggregate statistics, and that the labs are spending far ahead of revenue. The empirical question that will resolve is whether firms restructured around human-agent systems show measured productivity or margin gains that survive audit — the observable is sectoral productivity and headcount-per-unit-output data, plus whether AI-native firms keep those structures once compute is priced at cost rather than subsidised. The residue is worldview: Whittemore treats the practitioners living it as the best available evidence; Zitron treats first-person accounts from people selling the future as inadmissible. Whittemore is vindicated if the new organisational forms persist and spread beyond the essayists' own companies; Zitron if they turn out to have been a function of cheap tokens and end when the subsidy does. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: neither claims the labour-market data currently shows anything much. Watch what happens to those firms when inference is repriced.
